_README: Musical content for the genre paths. verified is true only when the tunings, scales, voicings, progressions, and lesson sentences were checked against that genre's sources. A band is named only when one of those sources names them.

genres.name: Blues
genres.blurb: Dominant 7ths on I, IV, and V, the 12-bar form, and minor-pentatonic and blues-scale soloing.

lessons.title: Dominant 7ths on I, IV, and V
lessons.explainer: The simplest 12-bar chart is the triads I, IV, and V. In practice, dominant 7th chords — root, major 3rd, 5th, and ♭7 — are generally used on all three. E Mixolydian is the E major scale with that ♭7 (E F# G# A B C# D), so it contains every note of E7.
lessons.practice: Play E7, A7, and B7 in time and listen for the ♭7 in each chord.

lessons.title: Minor pentatonic and the blues scale
lessons.explainer: The E minor pentatonic is E G A B D (1, ♭3, 4, 5, ♭7). The six-note blues scale adds the ♭5, B♭. Blue notes are commonly the ♭3, ♭5, and ♭7, and one blues scale is often used over the whole 12-bar form rather than a new scale on every chord.
lessons.practice: Play the E blues scale around the 12th fret and bend into the ♭5 instead of sitting on it.

lessons.title: The 12-bar form
lessons.explainer: The basic form is four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, V. The V in bar 12 leads back to the top. Quick to four puts IV in bar 2 and, in the usual chart, ends on I. Bars 9–12 (V–IV–I–V) are the turnaround, not a separate three-chord loop. This lesson uses the dominant-7th version of the basic form.
lessons.practice: Comp the 12 bars slowly, then try the same chords with a shuffle feel.

lessons.title: Open G and Open E for slide
lessons.explainer: Open G is D–G–D–G–B–D, low to high. The open strings are a G major chord, and barring one fret plays the other major chords, which is why slide and steel sit well in the tuning. It is common in blues and folk. Open E is E–B–E–G#–B–E, an E major chord, and is used the same way for slide.
lessons.practice: Tune to Open G, strum the open strings, then barre the 5th and 7th frets.

genres.name: Rock
genres.blurb: Power chords, Drop D, and minor-pentatonic and Mixolydian leads.

lessons.title: Power chords
lessons.explainer: A power chord is the root and the 5th, sometimes with an octave of either. There is no 3rd, so it is neither major nor minor. Under distortion a full triad's 3rd makes the sound muddy; the root and 5th stay clearer. The same shape moves up the neck.
lessons.practice: Play E5, A5, and D5 with a short palm mute so the chords stay percussive.

lessons.title: Drop D power
lessons.explainer: Drop D lowers only the low E to D, so the tuning is D A D G B E. The three open bass strings are a D5, and barring those three strings with one finger plays the other power chords. In standard tuning the same shape needs two or three fingers.
lessons.practice: Tune to Drop D and barre the low three strings at frets 0, 3, and 5.

lessons.title: The Mixolydian ♭VII
lessons.explainer: The loop on screen is I–♭VII–IV: E, D, and A in E major. ♭VII is the subtonic. E Mixolydian is E major with a ♭7 (D instead of D#), so this loop never uses the leading tone. That is a different sound from a V–I cadence. In G major, vi–IV–I–V is Em–C–G–D, a rotation of the common I–V–vi–IV loop.
lessons.practice: Loop E–D–A and notice that D does not pull the way a B7 would.

lessons.title: Minor pentatonic over a major vamp
lessons.explainer: E minor pentatonic is E G A B D. Over the E–D–A vamp, G is the ♭3 against an E major I chord. That ♭3 is a blue note; the clash is the usual rock-lead color, not a wrong note to avoid.
lessons.practice: Solo over E–D–A with only E minor pentatonic, and land on E, A, or D on the downbeats.

genres.name: Folk
genres.blurb: Open chords in G, the I–V–vi–IV loop, and DADGAD.

lessons.title: Open chords: G, C, D
lessons.explainer: In G major, I–IV–V is G, C, and D. The open-position shapes leave strings ringing, which is the usual first folk strum in this key. The relative minor, Em, is the vi chord.
lessons.practice: Change between G, C, and D in a steady down-up strum without stopping the pulse.

lessons.title: G major and its pentatonic
lessons.explainer: G major is G A B C D E F#. The G major pentatonic keeps G A B D E and leaves out the half steps (C and F#). Both collections stay inside the key of the G, C, D, and Em chords.
lessons.practice: Play G major in open position, then play it again skipping C and F#.

lessons.title: I–V–vi–IV
lessons.explainer: I–V–vi–IV in G is G–D–Em–C. It is a very common four-chord loop in folk and pop. The vi chord, Em, is the minor color before IV returns toward the tonic. I–vi–IV–V (G–Em–C–D) uses the same four chords in another order.
lessons.practice: Loop G–D–Em–C and sing a simple melody on the G major pentatonic.

lessons.title: DADGAD
lessons.explainer: From standard tuning, the 1st, 2nd, and 6th strings each drop a whole step, giving D A D G A D. Those open notes are D, G, and A: a Dsus4, so the open chord is neither major nor minor. Davey Graham popularized the tuning; it is most associated with Celtic music and is also used in folk. D Mixolydian (D E F# G A B C) matches that modal color: major, with a ♭7 and no leading tone.
lessons.practice: Tune to DADGAD, let the open strings ring, then move a one- or two-finger shape up the neck while a D or A string drones.

genres.name: Jazz
genres.blurb: ii–V–I with seventh chords, plus Dorian on the ii and Mixolydian on the V.

lessons.title: The ii–V–I cadence
lessons.explainer: In C major the jazz ii–V–I is Dm7–G7–Cmaj7. The 3rd and 7th of Dm7 are F and C; C falls a half step to B, the 3rd of G7, and F becomes the ♭7 of G7. That ♭7, F, then falls a half step to E, the 3rd of Cmaj7, while B becomes the major 7th. G13 keeps the same B–F tritone and adds the 9th (A) and 13th (E). In A minor the cadence is Bm7♭5–E7–Am7. The I–vi–ii–V turnaround in C is Cmaj7–Am7–Dm7–G7.
lessons.practice: Comp Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 and keep F moving to E on the way into Cmaj7.

lessons.title: Major 7th on I
lessons.explainer: Cmaj7 is C E G B: a major triad plus the major 7th. In a major-key ii–V–I, that is the usual I chord.
lessons.practice: Play Cmaj7, then a plain C triad, and listen for the B against the C.

lessons.title: Dorian over the ii chord
lessons.explainer: D Dorian is D E F G A B C: a D minor scale with a natural 6th, B, instead of B♭. The chord tones of Dm7 are D, F, A, and C, all inside that scale.
lessons.practice: Improvise over Dm7 in D Dorian and land on D, F, A, or C.

lessons.title: Mixolydian over the V chord
lessons.explainer: G Mixolydian is G A B C D E F: G major with a ♭7. Those notes include the chord tones of G7 (G, B, D, F). The ♭7 is the note that falls to E when the cadence resolves to Cmaj7.
lessons.practice: Play G Mixolydian over G7, then resolve F to E, the 3rd of Cmaj7.

genres.name: Metal
genres.blurb: Palm-muted power chords, Drop C, Phrygian ♭2 riffs, and harmonic minor as a separate color.

lessons.title: Palm-muted power chords
lessons.explainer: A power chord is the root and 5th, with no 3rd, so it is neither major nor minor and stays clear under distortion. Palm muting rests the picking hand at the bridge and turns the chord into a short percussive attack. That combination is a standard metal rhythm sound.
lessons.practice: Palm-mute E5 in steady eighth notes, then accent some of the attacks.

lessons.title: Drop C
lessons.explainer: Drop C, most commonly C G C F A D, is Drop D transposed down a whole step (or D standard with the 6th string dropped to C). The three lowest open strings, C G C, are a C5, so one finger still plays power chords. The lower pitch is why the tuning is common in rock and heavy metal.
lessons.practice: Tune to Drop C and barre the low three strings, muting the strings between hits.

lessons.title: Phrygian and harmonic minor
lessons.explainer: E Phrygian is E F G A B C D: a minor scale whose 2nd is only a half step above the root. E harmonic minor is a different collection, E F# G A B C D#. It is natural minor with a raised 7th, so it has a leading tone and does not have Phrygian's ♭2. In E minor, i–VI–VII is Em–C–D and i–iv–VII is Em–Am–D.
lessons.practice: Riff on the low strings in E Phrygian and lean on F, the ♭2. Then play D# once so you can hear the harmonic-minor leading tone.

lessons.title: The Phrygian i–♭II move
lessons.explainer: In E natural minor the diatonic II is F#. Flattening it gives F, a major chord a half step above Em. That i–♭II move is the chord form of Phrygian's ♭2. The power-chord version is E5 to F5.
lessons.practice: Palm-mute Em, then move up one fret to F. Try the same roots as E5 and F5.

genres.name: Funk
genres.blurb: Sixteenth-note guitar, dominant 9ths, and short one- or two-chord vamps.

lessons.title: The dominant 9th
lessons.explainer: Funk guitar favors extended chords, including dominant 9ths, and often plays them as short sixteenth-note stabs with muted ghost notes. E9 is E G# B D F#: root, 3rd, 5th, ♭7, and 9th. The verse of Wild Cherry's "Play That Funky Music" is mainly an E ninth chord. A dominant 7th with a ♯9, such as E7#9, is the related "Hendrix chord" color; funk harmony also uses sharp ninths.
lessons.practice: Strum E9 in sixteenths. Let a few attacks ring and mute the rest with the fretting hand.

lessons.title: Space, sixteenths, and the blues scale
lessons.explainer: Funk treats the rests between notes as part of the groove, and its guitar and drum parts often move in sixteenth notes so other parts can play more broken, syncopated rhythms. James Brown's groove emphasizes beat one ("the one"), not a rule that every rest sits on an off-beat. Funk bass lines often use blues-scale notes. E minor pentatonic is E G A B D; the E blues scale adds the ♭5, B♭.
lessons.practice: Play short E minor pentatonic notes over one chord. Leave gaps, and put a clear accent on beat one.

lessons.title: One chord or two
lessons.explainer: Unlike bebop's fast changes, funk often sits on one chord or on a two-chord vamp for a whole section. A documented pair is a minor seventh moving to the dominant seventh a fourth up, such as A minor to D7. In A minor that is i7–IV7, Am7–D7. The same pair in E is Em7–A7.
lessons.practice: Vamp Am7–D7 in sixteenths, then try Em7–A7.

lessons.title: Dorian on the minor vamp
lessons.explainer: E Dorian is E F# G A B C# D: E natural minor with a raised 6th. A7 contains C#, that raised 6th, so Em7–A7 agrees with E Dorian rather than with E natural minor (whose 6th is C).
lessons.practice: Solo over Em7–A7 in E Dorian and land on C# over the A7.

genres.name: Math Rock
genres.blurb: Odd and changing meters, tapping, extended chords, and open tunings such as FACGCE.

sources.title: Guitar World — Mike Kinsella on FACGCE

lessons.title: Odd and changing meters
lessons.explainer: Most rock stays in 4/4. Math rock uses uneven meters such as 5/4, 7/8, 11/8, and 13/8, and it changes meter, with irregular stops and starts. The chords below are an ordinary I–V–vi–IV in C (C–G–Am–F). The player in this app does not switch the click to an odd meter; you count the grouping yourself.
lessons.practice: Loop C–G–Am–F while counting 7/8 as 2+2+3. Then try 5/4 as 3+2 over the same chords.

lessons.title: FACGCE
lessons.explainer: FACGCE is F A C G C E, low to high (F2 A2 C3 G3 C4 E4). Mike Kinsella told Guitar World that the last two Cap'n Jazz songs were in this tuning, which Victor Villarreal had found, and that he learned it from Villarreal. American Football, the band he later played in, used many tunings; this is not a claim that every song of theirs is FACGCE. The open strings are F, A, C, E, and G: an Fmaj9.
lessons.practice: Tune to FACGCE and strum the open strings. Compare that sound with a fretted Fmaj9 in standard tuning.

lessons.title: Extended chords
lessons.explainer: Math rock guitar parts use extended chords rather than only triads. Cmaj7 is C E G B, a major triad plus the major 7th. Fmaj7 is F A C E. Fmaj9 adds the 9th, G, which is the chord the open FACGCE strings already spell. In C major, Imaj7–IVmaj7–vi7–V is Cmaj7–Fmaj7–Am7–G.
lessons.practice: Play Cmaj7, then Fmaj7, and name the 7th of each chord (B, then E).

lessons.title: Tapping on a diatonic line
lessons.explainer: Math rock guitarists use two-hand tapping to build on the drums' rhythms. Battles is the example usually given; tapping is a technique in the style, not something every math-rock band does on every song. A C major scale (C D E F G A B) stays inside the chords from the other lessons.
lessons.practice: Tap a short C major phrase with both hands, then play the same notes with a pick so you can hear that the pitches did not change.

genres.name: Djent
genres.blurb: Extended-range and dropped tunings, palm-muted syncopated low-string riffs, and polymeter.

lessons.title: Seven-string standard
lessons.explainer: Djent commonly uses seven- and eight-string guitars. Seven-string standard is B1 E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4: a low B under the usual six strings. Wikipedia names Trivium (on The Crusade and Shogun), Dream Theater, and Haken as bands that commonly use this tuning. Polyphia's Tim Henson has a seven-string signature, the Ibanez TOD70. That Guitar World report is about the guitar, not a published tuning for a specific song, so this preset is not credited to a Polyphia track.
lessons.practice: Use this tuning, then play the open 7th string against the open 6th. They are B and E, a fourth, the same interval as the low pair in six-string standard.

lessons.title: Drop A
lessons.explainer: Dropped A is A1 E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4: only the low B moves down a whole step to A. Wikipedia notes that many jazz players use it for bass lines and easier power chords. The three lowest strings, A E A, are an A5, so one finger barres them, as in Drop D on a six-string. No source checked here assigns this exact tuning to Polyphia or Unprocessed.
lessons.practice: Tune to Drop A and barre the lowest three strings at frets 0, 1, and 3.

lessons.title: Eight-string standard and Drop E
lessons.explainer: Eight-string standard is F# B E A D G B E, low to high (F#1 under seven-string standard). Tuning that F# down to E1 is Drop E: E1 B1 E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4. E1 is the low E of a four-string bass, and the relationship is the same as Drop D on a six-string. Wikipedia associates the eight-string with the djent sound of Meshuggah, Vildhjarta, and Periphery, and says Animals as Leaders primarily use drop E. Unprocessed have recorded with eight-string Ibanez guitars (an RG8 on Artificial Void; an RG Custom as the main guitar for And Everything In Between). Tim Henson has said newer Polyphia writing uses a lot of eight-string guitars and baritones. Neither interview states the open pitches, so those bands are not tied to this preset.
lessons.practice: Use Drop E and fret a one-finger power chord on the lowest three strings. Then switch to eight-string standard and hear the low string rise to F#.

lessons.title: Palm mutes and polymeter
lessons.explainer: Djent is named for the sound of a heavily distorted, palm-muted guitar chord. The style uses syncopated riffs and polymeter: a guitar grouping that does not match the bar the drums are counting, as on Animals as Leaders' "Cafo". There is no single djent scale. B Phrygian (B C D E F# G A) is one dark choice, because the ♭2 sits a half step above the low B of seven-string standard. In B minor, i–♭II is Bm–C.
lessons.practice: In seven-string standard, palm-mute an open B5. Accent every third sixteenth note while you keep counting a steady group of four.

genres.name: Alternative Metal
genres.blurb: Downtuned mid-paced riffs, minor-key grooves, and loud/quiet contrast.

lessons.title: Drop D groove riffs
lessons.explainer: Alternative metal is associated with heavily downtuned, mid-paced "chug" riffs. Drop D (D A D G B E) makes a D5 from the three open bass strings, and one finger plays the other power chords. Helmet used Drop D a great deal and influenced later alternative metal. Their own riffs are described as repetitive, syncopated, and staccato, often in a minor key, in Drop D or Drop C.
lessons.practice: Tune to Drop D. Palm-mute a one-finger D5 on the low three strings in a slow, even eighth-note chug, and accent beats 1 and the "and" of 2.

lessons.title: Drop C, a step lower
lessons.explainer: Drop C (C G C F A D) is Drop D down a whole step. It is the usual meaning of "Drop C", and it is common in rock and metal because the lower open strings sound heavier. The one-finger power-chord shape does not change. Helmet's write-ups name both Drop D and Drop C; this lesson does not assign either tuning to a specific Helmet song.
lessons.practice: Tune to Drop C and play the same low-three-string barre you used in Drop D. The fingering is the same; the pitch is a whole step lower.

lessons.title: A minor-key groove
lessons.explainer: Helmet's riffs are described as almost always in a minor key. In D minor, i–VII–VI is Dm–C–B♭ and i–iv–VII is Dm–Gm–C. D natural minor is D E F G A B♭ C. In E minor, i–VI–VII is Em–C–D. Power-chord versions of the roots are D5, C5, and E5.
lessons.practice: In Drop D, play Dm–C–B♭ as a slow loop. Mute the strings between chords so the changes stay tight.

lessons.title: Quiet, then loud
lessons.explainer: Deftones' Around the Fur is described as alternative metal (among other labels) and was praised for its loud/soft dynamics and for the rhythm-section groove. The contrast is dynamic, not a special chord: the same Em can be played clean and quiet, then palm-muted and harder. This lesson does not claim a tuning for that album.
lessons.practice: Fingerpick Em with no gain. Then play the same shape as short muted hits at a louder dynamic.
